column3: The second group has greater relative dispersion because its SD 15 exceeds 10, irrespective of the different means.

column3: Positive unit rescaling multiplies correlation by the same factor as covariance.

column2: For equally weighted observations X=-1,0,1 and Y=1,0,1, covariance is zero despite the deterministic relation Y=X squared.
column3: Zero covariance in that dataset establishes statistical independence of X and Y.

column3: Regression slopes 2 and 0.8 are admissible because each regression slope may individually exceed one.

column3: That fitted line has intercept 20 because the mean of Y is the intercept regardless of the mean of X.

column3: The reverse slope must be 2/3 because reversing the variables always inverts the forward slope.

column3: The same independence assumption gives union 0.9 because independent events are mutually exclusive.

column2: Mutually exclusive events with probabilities 0.3 and 0.4 have zero intersection and therefore are not independent.
column3: Those exclusive events are independent because knowing one occurred gives no information about the other.

column2: A rare-source prior can materially change a posterior even with high conditional likelihood; P(source given evidence) cannot generally be substituted by P(evidence given source).
column3: A conditional likelihood of 90% establishes a posterior of 90% regardless of the source's prior probability and other sources' likelihoods.

column3: Those parameters give variance 2 because variance always equals the mean in a binomial model.

column3: P(X at least 1)=2 exp(-2) because exactly-one and at-least-one probabilities are interchangeable.

column2: For suitable independent finite-variance observations, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as n grows; the individual observations need not become normally distributed.
column3: A large n makes the original skewed population itself normal under the central limit theorem.

column2: With unchanged finite population SD and independent draws, reducing the mean's standard error to one-half requires quadrupling the sample size.
column3: Doubling the sample size halves the mean's standard error because SE is inversely proportional to n.

column2: Under its assumptions, a 95% frequentist interval procedure covers the fixed population parameter in 95% of repeated samples; the realised interval either covers it or does not.
column3: For a realised frequentist interval, exactly 95% of population observations must fall inside it.

column3: A significant F in that design identifies every one of the six group pairs as significantly different without further comparisons.

column3: That expected count is 70 because independence expected frequencies are obtained by adding the marginal totals.

column2: Mann-Whitney compares two independent groups' rank distributions; interpreting it specifically as a median or location test requires suitable shape assumptions, while Kruskal-Wallis extends independent-group rank comparison.
column3: Mann-Whitney tests only median equality under any distribution shapes, and Kruskal-Wallis is the standard paired repeated-measures extension.
